s: Part five.
The built-in tools.
By the end of this part, you'll know exactly what each of Claude Code's six built-in tools does.
How to explore a big codebase without drowning in it.
And what you give up when you reach for the shell instead.
The plain picture.
A kitchen drawer holds a bread knife, a peeler, and a pair of scissors.
A decent pocket knife does all three jobs.
So the drawer looks like sentiment.
Why does it survive?
Two reasons.
First.
Each dedicated tool does its own job better.
Second.
When someone watches you pick up the peeler, they know roughly what's about to happen.
Watching you reach for the pocket knife tells them nothing.
Claude Code's six built-in tools are the drawer.
And Bash is the pocket knife.
The exam's real target isn't that these tools exist.
It's what you give up by reaching past them.
So here's each tool, precisely.
Six of them.
One.
Read.
It returns file contents with line numbers, and expects absolute paths.
When a file is too big, it returns the first page, with a partial-view notice explaining how to continue, using offset and limit.
It renders images.
It reads PDFs in page ranges.
It returns notebook cells with outputs.
And it does not read directories.
Two.
Write.
It creates a file, or overwrites it entirely.
No append.
No merge.
And overwriting an existing file requires having read it in the conversation.
Three.
Edit.
It replaces an exact old_string with a new_string.
There's no regular expression, and no fuzzy matching.
Three checks gate it.
The file must have been read. old_string must match byte for byte, including whitespace.
And it must appear exactly once, unless replace_all is set to true.
Four.
Grep.
It searches file contents.
It's built on ripgrep.
So it uses ripgrep's regular expression syntax, not traditional grep's.
That means literal braces need escaping.
It has three output modes. files_with_matches, the default, which returns paths only. content, which returns matching lines, with file and line numbers.
And count.
You can scope it by a file pattern, or by language type.
And you can turn on multiline, to match across lines.
It respects .gitignore, unless you pass an ignored path directly.
Five.
Glob.
It finds files by name pattern, with a double star for recursion.
Results are sorted by modification time, and capped at one hundred files.
There's a truncation flag, so Claude can narrow the pattern.
And unlike Grep, Glob ignores .gitignore by default.
Six.
Bash.
It runs commands, each in a separate process.
The working directory carries over within the project.
But environment variables do not.
Aliases and functions from your shell startup file are available, because Claude Code sources that file at session start.
Output is bounded.
Roughly thirty thousand characters for a successful result.
And ten thousand for a failure.
First concept.
Explore incrementally.
Picture finding every page of a thick manual that mentions a recalled part.
You use the index, and open only those pages.
Reading the whole manual first leaves you too tired to fix anything.
And flipping through the chapter titles won't show you where the part is mentioned.
Question one.
Here's the scenario.
An agent must replace every call to a deprecated legacyAuth function, in a monorepo of about four thousand files.
It currently globs every source file, and reads each in full before planning.
And it runs out of context before touching the first call site.
What should it do instead?
Take a second.
The answer.
Grep for the function name followed by an opening parenthesis, to list the files.
Read only the relevant regions.
Then Edit each call site.
The technical name is incremental exploration.
Let Grep tell you what to read.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: read every file under the source folder first.
Why?
That's the named anti-pattern of bulk reading.
Irrelevant files fill the context window before any reasoning starts.
Wrong: run grep through Bash, save the output to a file, and read that whole file.
Why?
It routes a search through the unconstrained shell.
And it loses Grep's structured output, truncation signal, and precise permission matching.
Wrong: glob all TypeScript files, then read each one.
Why?
That's still bulk reading.
Glob matches names, never contents.
So it cannot locate call sites.
"Read all the files first" is the classic distractor in this task statement.
Hold on to this line.
Grep says where, Read looks there, Edit changes only that.
Second concept.
When Edit fails.
Picture telling a painter to repaint "the blue door," on a street with seven blue doors.
You get confusion.
Or seven red doors.
"The blue door next to the bakery" gets exactly one done.
And knocking the house down and rebuilding it to change one door?
That's the other way to go wrong.
Question two.
Here's the scenario.
An agent must change a timeout of thirty to sixty, in the payments handler of a two-and-a-half-thousand-line configuration module.
The Edit call fails, because that exact timeout line appears seven times.
And only the payments handler should change.
On earlier tasks, full-file rewrites of this module silently dropped unrelated blocks.
What's the next move?
Take a second.
The answer.
Retry Edit, with old_string widened to include the payments handler's surrounding lines.
So it matches exactly once.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: replace_all set to true.
Why?
It changes all seven, including six handlers that must stay at thirty.
Wrong: read the whole module, and regenerate it with Write.
Why?
It reintroduces the dropped-code risk the stem warns about.
Wrong: a file-wide sed command through Bash.
Why?
It hits all seven occurrences.
And it moves a file edit into the shell, where permission rules match command strings, rather than intent.
Here's the third source disagreement.
The lesson nine deck says that when Edit fails, fall back to Read plus Write.
The notes say widen the anchor text first.
And treat Read plus Write as the fallback only when no unique anchor can be built.
The practice question sides with the notes.
And so should you.
If a stem says a unique anchor genuinely cannot be constructed, the fallback becomes legitimate.
And the stem phrase "full-file rewrites dropped code before" is there to steer you away from Write.
Hold on to this line.
When Edit finds too many matches, give it more context, not a bigger hammer.
Third concept.
Grep versus Glob, and the gitignore asymmetry.
Picture a records room with two clerks.
One reads the labels on the folders.
The other reads the documents inside.
Ask the label reader to find every letter that mentions a customer, and they can't.
Ask the document reader to find folders by name, and they're the wrong person too.
Each is fast and trustworthy at their own job.
Question three.
Here's the scenario.
A continuous integration agent has two jobs.
First, list every file named with the pattern star dot env dot example, including files under a generated folder that's listed in .gitignore.
Second, find every line in tracked source that mentions API_KEY.
The security team wants permission rules that name capabilities precisely, rather than match shell command strings.
Which tools should it use?
Take a second.
The answer.
Glob with a recursive pattern, for the file list.
And Grep in content mode, for the API_KEY lines.
Why does that work?
Glob sees the ignored generated folder, because it ignores .gitignore by default.
Grep respects .gitignore, which suits tracked source.
And both are narrow, read-only tools a permission rule can name directly.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: Grep for both.
Why?
Grep searches contents, not names.
And it would also skip the generated folder.
Wrong: Glob for both.
Why?
Glob never looks inside files.
Wrong: Bash, with find and grep.
Why?
It gets results, but fails the security constraint.
The constraint phrase is "name capabilities precisely."
And the asymmetry itself, that a file can be invisible to Grep and visible to Glob in the same repository, explains a lot of apparently inconsistent search results.
Hold on to this line.
Glob reads the labels and sees ignored files.
Grep reads the contents and respects .gitignore.
So why is Bash for search a design smell?
The exam expects all four reasons.
One.
You lose structure.
Grep returns typed modes.
Shell grep returns whatever lands on standard output, inside the Bash output budget.
Two.
You lose safety rails.
Grep and Glob are read-only, and do not prompt inside the working directory.
Bash prompts by default.
And once allowed, it's a general-purpose execution channel.
Three.
You lose enforceability.
A rule against Grep is precise.
A rule against Bash must pattern-match command strings.
And read and edit deny rules only cover file commands Claude Code recognises.
Four.
You lose tuned behaviour.
Truncation flags.
Gitignore semantics.
And ripgrep's diagnostics, which let the model fix a bad pattern and retry.
The notes have an item on this.
An agent granted Bash for grep and find gets silently truncated results.
It reports that a symbol does not exist, when it does.
And it leaves an audit that cannot show which paths were read.
The fix is to grant Read, Grep and Glob instead.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: Bash output is unbounded.
Why?
That's false.
Wrong: Glob searches contents.
Why?
That's also false.
Wrong: blame regular expression syntax.
Why?
It explains neither the truncation, nor the missing audit.
Bash stays necessary for jobs nothing narrower fits.
The discipline is to reach for it last.
Not because it's closest to hand.
Fourth concept.
What persists between Bash calls.
Picture ringing a call centre, and reaching a different agent each time.
The branch recorded on your account carries over.
But whatever you told the last agent out loud is gone.
If the next agent needs to know it, say it in the same call.
Question four.
Here's the scenario.
An agent runs export DEPLOY_ENV equals staging, in one Bash call.
Then it runs a preflight script, in the next call.
The script reports it's checking production.
That's its default when the variable is unset.
An earlier change of directory did carry over between the same two calls.
What's the cause, and what's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Each Bash call runs in a separate process.
So the export is lost.
The fix is to set the variable in the same command as the script.
Either inline, before the script name.
Or chained with a double ampersand.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: blame truncated output.
Why?
The script ran, and clearly reported which environment it used.
Wrong: claim the working directory also reset.
Why?
That contradicts the stem, which shows the directory change carried over.
Wrong: claim shell aliases are not loaded.
Why?
That's false.
Claude Code sources the startup file at session start.
Hold on to this line.
In Bash, the folder carries over, and the environment does not.
One naming collision to close.
Both product surfaces call their tools "built-in."
The six we just covered are Claude Code's built-in tools.
That's what this task statement names.
The Claude Developer Platform ships a separate built-in set.
There are server tools that run on Anthropic's infrastructure, such as web search, web fetch, code execution, and tool search.
And there are client tools you run yourself, such as memory, bash, and the text editor.
With computer use in beta.
Those carry dated version identifiers, and you pin a specific version.
So if an answer option contains a version string, treat it as a fact to check, not decoration.
That's part five.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
Use the narrow built-in tool that fits.
Grep, then Read, then Edit.
And reach for Bash last.
Coming up: the trap round.
The trap round.
Rapid fire.
Here's how it works.
I'll tell you what you might see in a question.
Then I'll tell you what to think.
If you see... think.
First, the traps from part one.
Descriptions, and the shape of tools.
If you see a system prompt rule naming which tool to use, think: fix the description instead, because that is where selection happens.
If you see a tool called repeatedly with rephrased arguments, think: the description never says what the tool does not return.
If you see "merge the tools" and the stem says the second tool is rarely needed, or slow and billed, think: do not merge.
If you see tools that are always called in sequence, think: consolidate into one.
If you see a parameter required only when another has a certain value, think: split the tool.
If you see plan and apply in one tool, and "cannot rely on instructions," think: split on risk, and withhold the risky tool.
If you see a hook versus withholding a tool, think: withholding is the top rung.
The hook is second.
If you see two near-synonym descriptions, and "lowest complexity" or "first," think: rename and bound.
Not a subagent, and not a classifier.
If you see a custom tool losing to Grep, think: better description first, examples second, routing last.
Next, the traps from part two.
Errors.
If you see an empty list returned on a timeout, think: silent failure.
Return isError true, transient.
If you see "please try again" on a denial, think: permission error.
Not retryable.
Name the scope.
Stop.
If you see "lower the retry cap," think: classification overrides the counter.
If you see a business rule returned as a JSON-RPC error, think: it reached your logic, so it belongs in a result.
If you see an unknown tool name, or an unparseable request, think: that one really is a protocol error.
If you see code parsing error prose with regular expressions, think: add structuredContent, and keep the prose.
If you see a coordinator aborting a whole run on one timeout, think: local bounded retry, structured escalation, keep partial results.
Now part three.
Distribution, and tool choice.
If you see a denylist over an inherited pool, think: it fails by omission.
Use an allowlist.
If you see tool_choice none used to stop one tool, think: it blocks every tool on that request.
If you see tool_choice any on every loop turn, think: it forces calls on summary turns.
Use auto.
If you see several acceptable schemas, and a need for a guaranteed call, think: any.
If you see one schema as the deliverable, think: name the tool.
If you see a large server that only one subagent uses, think: inline mcpServers in that subagent, not deferral.
If you see deferral offered for overlapping descriptions, think: deferral cuts cost.
It does not fix overlap.
Part four.
M C P servers.
If you see teammates missing a server that works for one developer, think: local scope.
Move it to .mcp.json.
If you see a committed header ignored, think: a local entry wins whole.
Remove it.
If you see a default value on a token, think: never.
Defaults go on endpoints.
If you see an authentication failure in continuous integration only, think: an unset variable was sent as literal text.
Inject the secret.
If you see an HTTP entry without a type, think: it is read as stdio, and skipped.
If you see a tool the agent fires on its own, when a person should start it, think: make it a prompt.
If you see "keeps fetching the wrong document," think: resources, with a stable address.
If you see readOnlyHint used to skip confirmation, think: annotations are untrusted.
Use permission rules and the tool set.
And part five.
The built-in tools.
If you see "read all files first," think: Grep, then Read, then Edit.
If you see Edit failing on a non-unique match, think: widen old_string.
Not replace_all.
Not Write.
If you see Glob used to search contents, or Grep used to find names, think: wrong clerk.
If you see Bash granted for search, think: lost structure, lost safety rails, lost enforceability, lost tuned behaviour.
If you see an exported variable missing in the next Bash call, think: separate processes.
Put it in the same command.
That's the trap round.
Coming up: the closing recap.
Ten things to remember.
The closing recap.
Ten things to remember from this chapter.
For each one, I'll give you the plain idea first.
Then the technical names to go with it.
One.
The model only knows what you wrote.
So the description is the interface.
And saying what a tool does not return is the most valuable sentence in it.
The technical name is the tool description, with a negative boundary, and a named next tool.
Two.
When two tools sound alike, fix the names and boundaries before adding any architecture.
The technical names are namespacing, mutually exclusive boundaries, and the misrouting ladder.
Rename, describe, examples, then classifiers.
Three.
Merge tools that always travel together.
Split tools that differ in risk, or in result shape, or that need a field only sometimes.
The technical names are consolidation, the action parameter, the god-tool anti-pattern, and conditional required parameters.
Four.
The strongest guarantee is not having the capability at all.
A code check comes second.
And an instruction is not a guarantee.
The technical name is the enforcement ladder.
Withhold, deny with a PreToolUse hook, validate a record.
Five.
Failures that reached your logic come back as results the model can read.
Only broken requests use the protocol's error channel.
The technical names are isError true, versus a JSON-RPC error object.
Six.
The kind of failure decides what happens next.
Not a retry counter.
The technical names are the error classes transient, business and permission.
The retryable field.
And the rule that classification overrides the counter.
Seven.
Give the model words, and give your code fields, side by side.
And recover locally before escalating.
The technical names are the content block, structuredContent with error_class and retryable, and bounded local retry with structured escalation.
Eight.
Give each agent the smallest bag of tools for its job.
And decide separately whether a request must end in a tool call.
The technical names are the tools allowlist, disallowedTools, inline mcpServers, and tool_choice, with auto, any, a named tool, or none.
Nine.
Shared servers live in the committed project file, with secrets pulled from the environment.
And each capability goes in the primitive that matches who decides.
The technical names are .mcp.json at project scope, and variable expansion with no default on secrets.
Then tools, resources and prompts, as model-controlled, application-driven, and user-controlled.
With annotations treated as untrusted.
Ten.
Use the narrow built-in tool that fits.
Search contents to find where, read only there, and change only that.
And remember what survives between shell calls.
The technical names are Grep then Read then Edit, a widened old_string, the gitignore asymmetry between Grep and Glob, and Bash keeping the working directory but not the environment.
That is Domain two.
In the next chapter, we move into Claude Code configuration and workflows.
That's where the hooks, permission rules and scopes we touched on here get their full treatment.
